the malignant clone in a case of Burkit's lymphoma could be identified in the peripheral blood and bone marrow using a third‐complementarily‐determining‐region (CDRIII)-specific molecular probe developed by sequencing DNA from a smear stored on a glass slide at room temperature for 1 year.

we have developed a clone‐specific molecular probe by PCR and sequencing DNA from a slide stored for more than one yean, which can be used for retrospective analysis of malignant cells in hematologic malignancies.

a method for molecular detection and monitoring of malignant cells in patients with Burkitt's lymphomas.
the development of a molecular probe for the detection of the malignant clone in a patient with Burkitt's lymphom.

the development of a new technique for detecting malignant cells by PCR amplification, using DNA from smears stored at room temperature, and with a retrospective study for malignant cells using a clone‐specific DNA probe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the third‐CDRIII sequence for the development of a probe is a useful method for the detection of the malignant clone in a case of B‐cell lymphoma.
the DNA extracted from a stored slide can be used as a template to amplify the IgH gene by PCR, and the amplified DNA can he sequenced.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a DNA sequence of the IgH variable gene from a frozen specimen was used as a template for development of a clone specific probe, which was used to detect a malignant clone on smears stored at room temperature.
a molecular analysis can be performed on a stored smear of a hematologic malignancy of B‐cell origin.

the DNA sequence of a smear stored at 25°C for more than 1 year could be used for PCR amplification and sequencing, and the DNA sequence obtained from a smear stored for 1 year was shown to be identical to that from a frozen sample.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DNA sequence of the IgH CDRIII can be obtained from DNA extracted from a stored slide.
DNA from a slide stored at room temperature can be used as a template for PCR and that the CDRIII sequence can be determined by sequencing.
it is possible to detect malignant cells in a stored blood sample by using a clone‐specific PCR assay.
